narrativeBlocks.title: Five hundred years later, same stories
narrativeBlocks.body: Ovid's Metamorphoses is the Roman re-telling: a poetic encyclopedia of transformation myths, written centuries after the Greek originals — and now, for many stories, our main surviving source.

narrativeBlocks.title: Different register entirely
narrativeBlocks.body: Where Greek tragedy is grave, Ovid is witty and nimble — he plays with the material, adds psychological depth, and tells the gods as vain, lecherous, petty characters as much as awe-inspiring ones.

narrativeBlocks.title: The stories we owe him
narrativeBlocks.body: Narcissus and Echo, Pyramus and Thisbe (the proto-Romeo and Juliet), Arachne's weaving contest, Daedalus and Icarus in full form, Apollo and Daphne — many of the 'Greek myths' you know best survive through Ovid's version.

narrativeBlocks.title: Transformation as the theme
narrativeBlocks.body: Ovid's unifying idea is change: people become trees, stars, birds, spiders. The shape-shifting is often the gods' mercy or punishment — metamorphosis as both escape and sentence.

narrativeBlocks.title: The pipeline to you
narrativeBlocks.body: Western art's mythology runs mostly through Ovid — Titian, Shakespeare, the whole Renaissance read him. Many 'original Greek' details you picture are actually Roman polish.
